title: Babylon between Assyria and Persia
subtitle: 1155–539 BC · The Revival under Nebuchadnezzar I, the Chaldean Centuries, the Assyrian Domination, and the Neo-Babylonian Empire

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The native revival under Nebuchadnezzar I, three centuries of Aramaean and Chaldean tribalisation, the long domination by Assyria, and the brief glory of the Chaldean empire under Nebuchadnezzar II before the fall to Cyrus

entries.label: Nebuchadnezzar I recovers Marduk from Elam
entries.hint: A native Babylonian dynasty rose from Isin on the wreck of the Kassites, and its greatest king, Nebuchadnezzar I, marched on Elam in the blistering heat of high summer, broke its army, and brought home the statue of Marduk that had sat in Susa for a generation. He became a national hero — and his reign is the likely moment when Marduk was formally elevated to king of the gods, celebrated in the Epic of Creation.
entries.note: J. A. Brinkman, 'A Political History of Post-Kassite Babylonia, 1158–722 B.C.' (1968); the Marduk-recovery poems; W. G. Lambert, 'Babylonian Creation Myths' (2013).

entries.label: The Aramaean and Chaldean centuries
entries.hint: For three hundred years Babylonia was weak and fragmented. Aramaean tribes overran the countryside and the marshes; a distinct people, the Chaldeans — Bit-Dakkuri, Bit-Amukani, Bit-Yakin — settled the deep south and became the strongest political force, several of their chiefs taking the throne of Babylon. The old cities shrank to temple-centred islands in a tribal sea, and 'no king' years, famine and Elamite raids fill the chronicles.
entries.note: J. A. Brinkman, 'A Political History of Post-Kassite Babylonia' (1968) and 'Prelude to Empire: Babylonian Society and Politics, 747–626 B.C.' (1984).

entries.label: Nabu-nasir and the start of the reliable record
entries.hint: From the accession of Nabu-nasir the Babylonian record turns continuous and trustworthy — not because his reign mattered, but because the apparatus stabilised. The king-list that the astronomer Ptolemy would use for his chronology begins here, and so do the continuous Astronomical Diaries. The 'era of Nabonassar' became the fixed point from which later astronomers counted back.
entries.note: E. J. Bickerman, 'Chronology of the Ancient World' (1980); the Ptolemaic Canon and the 'Nabonassar era'.

entries.label: Merodach-Baladan and the resistance to Assyria
entries.hint: Marduk-apla-iddina II, chief of the Chaldean tribe Bit-Yakin, seized the throne of Babylon twice and led the anti-Assyrian resistance with Elamite money and men. He sent an embassy to Hezekiah of Judah — the visit the book of Isaiah turns into a warning of exile. Sargon and then Sennacherib drove him back into the marshes each time. He became the symbol of Babylonian defiance.
entries.note: J. A. Brinkman, 'Merodach-Baladan II' (1964); the embassy in 2 Kings 20 and Isaiah 39.

entries.label: Babylon under the Sargonids — the see-saw and the ruin
entries.hint: Assyria tried everything with the south. Sennacherib installed a son (kidnapped by Elam), then a puppet, then in 689 razed Babylon and flooded the site. Esarhaddon rebuilt it in a theological reversal and split the empire, making his elder son Shamash-shum-ukin king of Babylon under his brother Ashurbanipal. The arrangement produced a civil war, and after it a puppet, Kandalanu, held the city in a graveyard peace.
entries.note: Grant Frame, 'Babylonia 689–627 B.C.: A Political History' (1992).

entries.label: Shamash-shum-ukin's revolt and the starving of Babylon
entries.hint: Esarhaddon's elder son, king of Babylon while his younger brother ruled Assyria, rose in 652 with Elamite, Arab and Chaldean allies. Ashurbanipal's army besieged Babylon and Sippar for years; the chronicle records people eating their own children. In 648 the city fell and Shamash-shum-ukin died in the flames of his palace. Babylonia was quiet for the next twenty years — the quiet of exhaustion.
entries.note: A. K. Grayson, 'Assyrian and Babylonian Chronicles' (1975); Jamie Novotny & Joshua Jeffers, RINAP 5 (2018).

entries.label: Nabopolassar founds the Neo-Babylonian Empire
entries.hint: As the Assyrian grip failed, a man of obscure origin — a Chaldean, or a provincial governor — took Babylon in 626 and fought a ten-year war of liberation. He allied with the Medes under Cyaxares, and the joint armies destroyed Assyria: Ashur in 614, Nineveh in 612, the last stand at Harran in 610. Nabopolassar founded the last empire that Mesopotamia would ever rule from within.
entries.note: Rocío Da Riva, 'The Inscriptions of Nabopolassar, Amel-Marduk and Neriglissar' (2013); the Babylonian Chronicles (Grayson 1975).

entries.label: Nebuchadnezzar II — the builder and the exile
entries.hint: Nebuchadnezzar II smashed Egypt at Carchemish in 605, inheriting the western empire, and then spent forty years rebuilding Babylon on a scale never seen — the Ishtar Gate, the Processional Way, the ziggurat Etemenanki, the double walls, the palaces with their terraced garden. He besieged Jerusalem twice, deporting its elite in 597 and, after a revolt, destroying the city and the Temple in 587 and deporting the rest — the exile out of which Judaism was made.
entries.note: D. J. Wiseman, 'Nebuchadrezzar and Babylon' (1985); Rocío Da Riva on the Nebuchadnezzar inscriptions; the Jerusalem sieges in 2 Kings 24–25.

entries.label: The unstable succession
entries.hint: Nebuchadnezzar's son Amel-Marduk — the 'Evil-Merodach' of the book of Kings, who freed the exiled Judahite king Jehoiachin from prison — was murdered within two years by his brother-in-law Neriglissar. Neriglissar reigned four years and campaigned in Cilicia; his boy son Labashi-Marduk was killed within months of his accession. The throne then passed clean out of the royal house.
entries.note: Rocío Da Riva, 'The Inscriptions of Nabopolassar, Amel-Marduk and Neriglissar' (2013); the Amel-Marduk notice in 2 Kings 25:27–30.

entries.label: Nabonidus and the moon-god
entries.hint: Nabonidus, an outsider whose mother had been a priestess of the moon-god Sin at Harran, promoted Sin over Marduk, rebuilt Sin's temple at Harran, restored ancient sanctuaries with an antiquarian's care — reading old inscriptions, digging up and dating foundation deposits — and then left Babylon for ten years to live at the Arabian oasis of Tayma, leaving his son Belshazzar as regent. The Marduk priesthood turned against him, and their account of his 'madness' is what survives.
entries.note: Paul-Alain Beaulieu, 'The Reign of Nabonidus, King of Babylon 556–539 B.C.' (1989); the Harran stelae and the 'Verse Account'.

entries.label: The fall to Cyrus
entries.hint: Cyrus the Persian, master already of Media and Lydia, defeated the Babylonian army at Opis in the autumn of 539, and days later his troops entered Babylon 'without a battle' — the priesthood, and perhaps the city, opening the gates. Cyrus proclaimed himself Marduk's chosen restorer of a Babylon misruled by Nabonidus. The last empire ruled by Mesopotamians ended, and the land became a province of others for the next twenty-four centuries.
entries.note: The Nabonidus Chronicle (ABC 7); the Cyrus Cylinder; Amélie Kuhrt, 'The Cyrus Cylinder and Achaemenid Imperial Policy' (JSOT 1983).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Nebuchadnezzar I's raid on Elam, the raids and famines of the dark age, the wars of resistance to Assyria, Nabopolassar's war of liberation, the sieges of Jerusalem and Tyre, and the fall at Opis

entries.label: Nebuchadnezzar I's summer raid on Elam
entries.hint: Nebuchadnezzar I marched on Elam in the worst of the summer heat — 'the axe blade burned like fire, the road scorched like flame', his poem says — surprised and broke the Elamite army on the Ulai river, and carried the statue of Marduk back to Babylon after decades in captivity. It was the one clear military triumph of the dark centuries, and it was remembered for a thousand years.
entries.note: The Nebuchadnezzar I 'Elamite' narrative texts; Brinkman, 'A Political History of Post-Kassite Babylonia' (1968).

entries.label: The raids and famines of the dark centuries
entries.hint: The chronicles of the tribal centuries are a litany of disaster: Aramaeans and Suteans 'the enemies of the Ekur' raiding the cities and cutting the New Year processions, Elamite incursions, years of no king, and repeated famine severe enough to break up the temple communities. Babylon's own akitu festival lapsed for decades at a time for want of a legitimate king to lead it.
entries.note: The 'Religious Chronicle' and the 'Chronicle of the Market Prices'; Brinkman (1968).

entries.label: The wars of resistance to Assyria
entries.hint: For a century Babylonia fought Assyrian domination in every way it could — Chaldean chiefs seizing the throne, Elamite armies hired as allies, city revolts, and the marshes as a refuge. Merodach-Baladan led it twice; Sennacherib answered by destroying Babylon in 689; Shamash-shum-ukin's revolt of 652 was the last great effort. Each round ended worse for the south than the last.
entries.note: Grant Frame, 'Babylonia 689–627 B.C.' (1992); the Assyrian side in the folio assyria-911bc-609bc.

entries.label: Nabopolassar and the destruction of Assyria
entries.hint: Nabopolassar's ten-year war expelled the Assyrians from Babylonia and then, in alliance with Cyaxares' Medes, went for the heart of the empire itself. Ashur fell in 614, Nineveh was stormed and burned in 612, and the last Assyrian king was crushed at Harran in 610 and at Carchemish, with Egyptian help, in 605. Babylon inherited Assyria's western empire in the process.
entries.note: The 'Fall of Nineveh Chronicle' and the 'Chronicle Concerning the Early Years of Nebuchadnezzar II' (Grayson 1975).

entries.label: Carchemish, Jerusalem and Tyre
entries.hint: At Carchemish in 605 Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the Egyptian army and made the Levant Babylonian. He besieged Tyre for thirteen years without taking it. And he twice besieged Jerusalem: in 597 he deported King Jehoiachin and the elite; in 587, after Zedekiah's revolt, he burned the city and the Temple, blinded the king, and deported the rest. The Babylonian Exile — the making of the Hebrew Bible — begins here.
entries.note: The Babylonian Chronicle for 605–594; 2 Kings 24–25; Jeremiah 39, 52; the sieges dated by the 'Jehoiachin ration tablets' from Babylon.

entries.label: Opis and the entry of Cyrus
entries.hint: In the autumn of 539 Cyrus met the Babylonian army at Opis on the Tigris and broke it, massacring the survivors. Sippar surrendered without a fight; two days later the general Ugbaru took Babylon itself, and Cyrus entered in state seventeen days after that. Nabonidus was captured; Belshazzar, by one tradition, killed. The last independent Mesopotamian state ended not in a great siege but in a walk-in.
entries.note: The Nabonidus Chronicle (ABC 7); the biblical dramatisation in Daniel 5 ('the writing on the wall').

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The temple as the surviving institution and the privileges of the citizen, the great Neo-Babylonian temple archives, the light-touch state ruling through the cities, building as statecraft, and Babylonian family law

entries.label: The boundary stone through the chaos
entries.hint: The kudurru — the inscribed stone recording a royal land grant with its gods called as guarantors — went on being carved right through the tribal centuries, and the grants track where power had gone: to the great temples, and to the Aramaean and Chaldean chiefs the crown needed to buy. The stone monument outlasted the kings whose gifts it recorded.
entries.note: Kathryn Slanski, 'The Babylonian Entitlement narûs (kudurrus)' (2003); Susanne Paulus, 'Die babylonischen Kudurru-Inschriften' (2014).

entries.label: The temple survives, and so does the citizen
entries.hint: Through every collapse the great temples endured — Esagila at Babylon, Ezida at Borsippa, Ebabbar at Sippar, Eanna at Uruk — holding the land, the archives, the calendar and a corporate identity no dynasty could destroy. And with them survived the mār Babili, the 'citizen': a legal status carrying tax exemption, freedom from conscription and from arbitrary flogging, and a voice in the city assembly. Every king, Chaldean or Persian, had to court it.
entries.note: The 'Advice to a Prince' text on citizen privileges; Michael Jursa on the Neo-Babylonian temple economy; A. Leo Oppenheim, 'Ancient Mesopotamia' (1964).

entries.label: The great Neo-Babylonian temple archives
entries.hint: Under the Chaldean empire the temples became huge bureaucratic estates, and their archives — tens of thousands of tablets from the Eanna at Uruk and the Ebabbar at Sippar — document them to the day: the prebends bought and sold, the oblates and rent-farmers, the herds and the date gardens, the loans, and the royal 'resident' (qīpu) watching over the whole for the crown, which taxed the temple rather than the people.
entries.note: Michael Jursa, 'Neo-Babylonian Legal and Administrative Documents' (2005); Kristin Kleber, 'Tempel und Palast: Die Beziehungen zwischen dem König und dem Eanna-Tempel' (2008).

entries.label: The light-touch empire
entries.hint: The Neo-Babylonian empire kept the Assyrian provincial framework in the conquered west, but ruled Babylonia itself through the temples and the city elites rather than a dense royal bureaucracy. It carved no palace reliefs, glorified no conquests: the king's inscriptions are almost entirely about building temples and canals. It was a deliberate self-presentation as the pious opposite of the Assyrian conqueror-state it had just destroyed.
entries.note: Paul-Alain Beaulieu, 'A History of Babylon, 2200 BC – AD 75' (2018); Rocío Da Riva on the Neo-Babylonian royal inscriptions.

entries.label: Building as the work of a king
entries.hint: Where an Assyrian king proved himself by conquest, a Babylonian king proved himself by restoration. Nebuchadnezzar II's inscriptions catalogue temples rebuilt, walls raised, gates faced with glazed brick, canals dug and processional ways paved — the ruler as the servant who keeps the gods' houses in repair. It is a whole alternative theory of what royal legitimacy is made of.
entries.note: Rocío Da Riva, 'The Twin Inscriptions of Nebuchadnezzar at Brisa' (2012); Andrew George, 'Babylonian Topographical Texts' (1992).

entries.label: Marriage, dowry and the Babylonian family
entries.hint: The Neo-Babylonian legal documents are dense with private life: marriage agreements specifying the dowry and the wife's continued control of it, adoptions used to move property, apprenticeship contracts binding a boy to a weaver or a seal-cutter for years, slave sales, and lawsuits over all of it. A fragmentary 'Neo-Babylonian Laws' text survives, but the living law is in the thousands of contracts of the city's propertied families.
entries.note: Martha Roth, 'Babylonian Marriage Agreements, 7th–3rd Centuries B.C.' (1989); Cornelia Wunsch on the family archives.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Marduk raised to king of the gods in the Epic of Creation, the New Year that remakes the world, the Judean exile and the making of Judaism, the multi-ethnic city, mathematical astrology, and Nabonidus and the moon-god

entries.label: Marduk becomes king of the gods
entries.hint: The Epic of Creation, Enuma Elish, tells how Marduk alone dared face the chaos-ocean Tiamat, killed her, split her body into sky and earth, set the stars and the calendar, made humanity from the blood of a rebel god, and was proclaimed king by the assembly of the gods, who recited his fifty names. It is a theological revolution — the local god of one city made the supreme power of the universe — probably composed to celebrate Nebuchadnezzar I's recovery of Marduk's statue.
entries.note: W. G. Lambert, 'Babylonian Creation Myths' (2013).

entries.label: The New Year that remakes the world
entries.hint: For eleven days each spring, Marduk's statue left the Esagila and processed down the Processional Way, out through the Ishtar Gate, to the akitu-house outside the walls, the gods of the other cities brought to attend. Enuma Elish was recited; the king was humiliated and re-invested; and the destinies of the coming year were 'fixed'. The festival was the annual re-enactment of creation and the renewal of royal and cosmic order. Without a legitimate king it could not be held.
entries.note: Julye Bidmead, 'The Akitu Festival' (2002); the procession route in Andrew George, 'Babylonian Topographical Texts' (1992).

entries.label: The exile and the making of Judaism
entries.hint: The Judeans deported in 597 and 587 were settled in villages in the Babylonian countryside — the 'al-Yahudu', Judah-town, tablets record their farming, their loans, their names. Among them, priest-scribes confronting the loss of the Temple produced the core of the Hebrew Bible: the Priestly source, Ezekiel, the explicit monotheism of Second Isaiah, and the edited Torah. Out of the catastrophe came a portable, text-centred religion whose god was not bound to a land.
entries.note: Rainer Albertz, 'Israel in Exile' (2003); Laurie Pearce & Cornelia Wunsch, 'Documents of Judean Exiles and West Semites in Babylonia' (2014).

entries.label: The many peoples of Babylon
entries.hint: Nebuchadnezzar's Babylon held deportees and hostages from everywhere — a single set of ration tablets names oil issued to the exiled Judahite king Jehoiachin, to Phoenician sailors, to Egyptian and Elamite craftsmen, and to 'Ionian' (Greek) carpenters and shipwrights. It was a genuinely multi-ethnic capital, the largest city in the world, its streets carrying a dozen languages beneath the official Akkadian and the everyday Aramaic.
entries.note: The 'Weidner ration tablets' from Babylon (Ernst Weidner, 1939); Pearce & Wunsch (2014).

entries.label: Astrology becomes a mathematical science
entries.hint: The Neo-Babylonian and early Persian centuries are when Babylonian astronomy became genuinely predictive: the scholars of the Esagila and the Resh temple worked out the cycles well enough to forecast eclipses, new moons and planetary positions, invented the twelve-sign zodiac around 500 BC, and cast the first personal horoscopes from about 410. The omen watched for the king was becoming a calculation made for a client.
entries.note: Francesca Rochberg, 'The Heavenly Writing' (2004) and 'Babylonian Horoscopes' (1998).

entries.label: Nabonidus and the piety of the past
entries.hint: Nabonidus elevated the moon-god Sin over Marduk, rebuilt Sin's ruined temple at Harran, and pursued an antiquarian's devotion — restoring ancient sanctuaries by their original plans, reading old royal inscriptions, and digging up, cleaning and dating a foundation deposit of Naram-Sin of Akkad (he was off by centuries, but the method was real). To the Marduk priesthood of Babylon it looked like heresy, and their hostile 'Verse Account' is the version that came down.
entries.note: Paul-Alain Beaulieu, 'The Reign of Nabonidus' (1989); the Naram-Sin deposit in the Nabonidus cylinder from the Ebabbar.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Ishtar Gate and the Processional Way, the ziggurat Etemenanki, the Epic of Creation as literature, the scholarly cult of the deep past, and the anti-Assyrian royal image

entries.label: The Ishtar Gate and the Processional Way
entries.loc: Found: Babylon · Now: Pergamon Museum, Berlin (reconstructed)
entries.hint: Nebuchadnezzar's northern gate and the avenue leading to it were faced with glazed brick: a deep lapis-blue ground carrying rows of striding lions along the Way, and bulls and slender horned dragons on the Gate, moulded in relief and glazed yellow and white. It is the summit of a nine-hundred-year Mesopotamian tradition of the coloured brick facade. The excavated fragments were shipped to Berlin and rebuilt at a fraction of the original scale.
entries.note: Robert Koldewey, 'Das Ischtar-Tor in Babylon' (1918); Joachim Marzahn, 'The Ishtar Gate, the Processional Way, the New Year Festival of Babylon' (2008).

entries.label: Etemenanki — the Tower of Babel
entries.hint: The ziggurat of Marduk, rebuilt by Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar, stood on a base ninety-one metres square and, by the measurements of the 'Esagil Tablet', rose about the same in height in seven receding stages, a stairway on the south face. It is the tower the biblical writers had in mind for the story of Babel — 'a tower with its top in the heavens', and the confusion of tongues. Later ages carted its bricks away; the site is now a reed-filled pit.
entries.note: Andrew George, 'The Tower of Babel: Archaeology, History and Cuneiform Texts' (AfO 2005/06); the 'Esagil Tablet' and the 'Tower of Babel Stele' of Nebuchadnezzar.

entries.label: The Epic of Creation as a work of art
entries.hint: Beyond its theology, Enuma Elish is a piece of virtuoso poetry: the slow build of cosmic menace, the failure of the older gods, Marduk's terms and his single combat with Tiamat, the assembly's acclamation, and the closing hymn that unpacks his fifty names one by one. It was recited whole at the New Year, adapted by the Assyrians with their own god in the lead role, and its ordered, waters-divided creation stands behind the first chapter of Genesis.
entries.note: W. G. Lambert, 'Babylonian Creation Myths' (2013); Benjamin Foster, 'Before the Muses' (2005).

entries.label: The cult of the deep past
entries.hint: Neo-Babylonian building and writing were deliberately archaic. Scribes revived Old Babylonian sign-forms and long-dead royal titles; kings 'restored' ancient temples to what they believed were their original plans, and searched for and re-buried the foundation inscriptions of their predecessors; the deep Mesopotamian past was treated as a canon to be recovered and imitated. It is a self-conscious classicism, two thousand years deep.
entries.note: Paul-Alain Beaulieu, 'Antiquarianism and the Concern for the Past in the Neo-Babylonian Period' (1994).

entries.label: The anti-Assyrian royal image
entries.hint: Where Assyrian kings covered their walls with scenes of slaughter, the Neo-Babylonian royal image is austere and frontal: on Nabonidus's Harran stele the king stands alone, staff in hand, beneath the emblems of the moon, the sun and the planet Venus, and the text beside him is about a temple. No enemies, no bodies, no narrative. The restraint is a statement — the pious king against the memory of the Assyrian conqueror.
entries.note: The Harran stelae (H1 B and H2) in Beaulieu, 'The Reign of Nabonidus' (1989); C. J. Gadd, 'The Harran Inscriptions of Nabonidus' (1958).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The invention of mathematical predictive astronomy, the zodiac and the personal horoscope, the exilic reconception of god and history, the classicism of the temple scholars, and the seven-century Astronomical Diaries

entries.label: Mathematical predictive astronomy
entries.hint: The Babylonian astronomers built a computational astronomy: purely arithmetical schemes — the 'System A' and 'System B' of the ephemeris tables — that predicted the moon's and the planets' positions, the dates of eclipses, and the lengths of the months, with no geometric model of the heavens at all. It was the most accurate predictive science anywhere before Ptolemy, and it is the direct ancestor of Greek and all later astronomy.
entries.note: Otto Neugebauer, 'A History of Ancient Mathematical Astronomy' (1975); Mathieu Ossendrijver, 'Babylonian Mathematical Astronomy: Procedure Texts' (2012).

entries.label: The zodiac and the personal horoscope
entries.hint: Around 500 BC the Babylonians divided the band of sky the sun travels into twelve equal thirty-degree signs — the zodiac, a mathematical grid distinct from the older constellations. And from about 410 BC they began casting horoscopes for individuals: the sky at the moment of a birth, read for the child's fortune. Astrology shifted from omens for the state to predictions for a person, and in that form it spread to Greece, Egypt, India and beyond.
entries.note: Francesca Rochberg, 'Babylonian Horoscopes' (1998); the zodiac's invention dated by Lis Brack-Bernsen and John Steele.

entries.label: The exilic reconception of god and history
entries.hint: The Judean scribes in Babylon, forced to explain a destroyed Temple and a god apparently defeated, produced a new theology and a new way of writing history: a single transcendent creator who has no image and no rival (Second Isaiah, arguing point by point against Babylonian idol-making), and a covenant history that reads the whole national catastrophe as a deserved punishment rather than a divine failure. The intellectual foundations of Judaism, and through it of Christianity and Islam, are laid in this exile.
entries.note: Rainer Albertz, 'Israel in Exile' (2003); Konrad Schmid, 'The Old Testament: A Literary History' (2012).

entries.label: The text as sacred and the commentary as knowledge
entries.hint: For the temple scholars, knowledge meant mastering a fixed corpus of canonical texts and unfolding their meaning in commentaries — line-by-line explanations linking an omen to its hidden sense by wordplay, analogy and cross-reference. The learned caste, 'the scribes of Enuma Anu Enlil', passed the disciplines down by family, guarded parts of them as secret, and treated the inherited text as the thing to be interpreted rather than tested.
entries.note: Eckart Frahm, 'Babylonian and Assyrian Text Commentaries' (2011); Alan Lenzi, 'Secrecy and the Gods' (2008).

entries.label: The Astronomical Diaries — seven centuries of data
entries.hint: From 747 BC the scholars of the Esagila kept a nightly record — the position of the moon and the planets, eclipses, meteors, haloes, the weather, the height of the Euphrates, the market price of barley, dates, wool and sesame, and the major events of the day. They kept it, with gaps, for nearly seven hundred years. It is the longest continuous scientific observation programme ever run, and the raw data on which the mathematical astronomy was built.
entries.note: Hermann Hunger & Abraham Sachs, 'Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia' (1988–2006); the price data analysed by R. J. van der Spek.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The temple estates at the economic core, the entrepreneurial banking families, the building boom of Nebuchadnezzar, the date economy of the south, and Babylon as the commercial hub of the Near East

entries.label: The temple estates at the core
entries.hint: The great temples were the largest economic units in the country: landholders of thousands of hectares, employers of oblates and hired men, keepers of herds in the tens of thousands, lenders of silver and grain, and rent-farmers of their own fields. The crown drew its Babylonian revenue mostly by taxing the temple — a lighter, more indirect fiscal system than the direct provincial extraction of Assyria.
entries.note: Michael Jursa, 'Aspects of the Economic History of Babylonia in the First Millennium BC' (2010); Kristin Kleber, 'Tempel und Palast' (2008).

entries.label: The entrepreneurial houses — the Egibi
entries.hint: Private business houses like the Egibi family of Babylon and, later, the Murashu of Nippur ran credit, land-leasing, tax-farming and long-distance trade across several generations, leaving archives of hundreds of tablets. They took deposits, issued interest-bearing notes payable to the bearer, formed partnerships, and financed the state's tax collection — a sophisticated commercial economy that fell not far short of banking.
entries.note: Cornelia Wunsch, 'Das Egibi-Archiv' (2000); Kathleen Abraham, 'Business and Politics under the Persian Empire' (2004) on the Murashu.

entries.label: Nebuchadnezzar rebuilds the largest city in the world
entries.hint: Nebuchadnezzar's forty-year building programme reshaped Babylon: the double walls and the moat, the eight gates, the Processional Way, three palaces, the ziggurat, and dozens of temples, using corvée and deportee labour, bitumen floated down from the Hit seeps, cedar hauled from Lebanon, and baked bricks stamped with the king's name by the million. It was the biggest construction project the ancient world had seen.
entries.note: Olof Pedersén, 'Babylon: The Great City' (2021); Rocío Da Riva on the building inscriptions.

entries.label: The date economy of the south
entries.hint: The recovered south under the Chaldean empire was a landscape of date-palm gardens laced with canals and bordered by marsh. The date was the staple food and a store of wealth: temple land was leased for a rent paid in dates, loans were reckoned in them, and the surplus moved north to feed Babylon. Barley grew between and beneath the palms. It is the agricultural pattern that defines the Iraqi south to the present.
entries.note: Michael Jursa, 'Aspects of the Economic History of Babylonia' (2010); Govert van Driel, 'Elusive Silver' (2002).

entries.label: Silver and the commercial hub
entries.hint: Babylonia ran on weighed silver — coinage came only slowly, with the Persians — and the price data in the Astronomical Diaries let its economy be tracked across centuries, the first ancient economy for which that is possible. Sitting astride the Tigris and Euphrates with the western empire's tribute flowing in, Babylon was the commercial pivot of the Near East, its markets moving Egyptian linen, Anatolian metal, Arabian incense and Iranian stone.
entries.note: Peter Vargyas, 'A History of Babylonian Prices in the First Millennium BC' (2001); Jursa (2010).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The glazed-brick facade at its peak, the double walls and the Median Wall, the canals and the terraced garden, and the instruments of the astronomers

entries.label: The glazed-brick facade at its peak
entries.hint: The Ishtar Gate and Processional Way pushed the moulded, coloured brick to its limit: bricks shaped to interlock into figures in relief, coated in alkaline glazes — including a newly available strong cobalt blue — and fired to a durable, weatherproof finish. It was the largest and most refined application of a technique that Mesopotamia had been developing since the Kassite temple of Uruk nine hundred years before.
entries.note: Robert Koldewey on the excavation; the glaze technology in Anton Moortgat and in Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994).

entries.label: The walls of Babylon and the Median Wall
entries.hint: Nebuchadnezzar ringed Babylon with a double circuit — Imgur-Enlil and Nimit-Enlil — a wide moat, and an outer wall enclosing a huge area of fields and reservoirs, meant to feed the city through a siege. Across the narrow neck of Mesopotamia north of the city he built a further barrier, the wall Xenophon's men would call the 'Median Wall', to hold off attack from the north. Herodotus's astonished (and inflated) account of Babylon's walls comes from this system.
entries.note: Robert Koldewey, 'Das wieder erstehende Babylon' (1913); Xenophon, 'Anabasis' II.4; Herodotus I.178–186.

entries.label: The canals and the terraced garden
entries.hint: Nebuchadnezzar's engineers cut canals linking the Tigris and Euphrates, built flood defences and reservoirs, and diverted the Euphrates itself to work on its bed. His Southern Palace held a raised, planted, irrigated terrace — the Babylonian tradition of the royal garden, and the reason the 'Hanging Gardens' were placed here, though the best-attested such garden is actually Sennacherib's at Nineveh.
entries.note: Nebuchadnezzar's canal inscriptions (Da Riva); the garden question in Stephanie Dalley, 'The Mystery of the Hanging Garden of Babylon' (2013).

entries.label: The instruments of the astronomers
entries.hint: The predictive astronomy rested on measurement: the water-clock to time an eclipse or the interval from sunset to moonrise, the gnomon and the shadow-table for the solstices, sighting along a fixed line to catch a star's culmination, and the systematic estimation of angular distance in 'cubits' and 'fingers'. Simple tools, but used with a consistency and over a span that no one had managed before.
entries.note: Otto Neugebauer, 'A History of Ancient Mathematical Astronomy' (1975); David Brown on Babylonian observational method.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The long cold war with Egypt over the Levant, the Median alliance and then the Median wall, Nabonidus's decade in the Arabian oases, the rise of Persia, and the Cyrus Cylinder's propaganda of liberation

entries.label: The long cold war with Egypt
entries.hint: Egypt was Babylon's rival for the Levant for half a century. Necho II tried to prop up dying Assyria and was smashed at Carchemish in 605; Egypt then backed one Judahite and Phoenician revolt after another against Babylonian rule, and Apries sent a force that briefly lifted the siege of Jerusalem in 588. Nebuchadnezzar campaigned toward the Egyptian border more than once. Neither power could dislodge the other, and the corridor stayed contested until the Persians took both.
entries.note: Anthony Spalinger, 'Egypt and Babylonia: A Survey' (1977); the Babylonian Chronicle for 605–594.

entries.label: The Medes — ally, then menace
entries.hint: Nabopolassar's alliance with Cyaxares' Medes destroyed Assyria and divided the spoils — Babylon took Mesopotamia and the west, Media the northern highlands. A marriage sealed it: Nebuchadnezzar and a Median princess whose homesickness, the Greek legend says, prompted the Hanging Gardens. But a strong Media on the northern frontier soon looked like a threat, and the 'Median Wall' was built with it in mind — until Cyrus removed the problem by conquering Media himself.
entries.note: Herodotus I.74, 185–186; the Nabopolassar–Cyaxares alliance in the Fall of Nineveh Chronicle; the marriage in Berossus (via Josephus).

entries.label: Nabonidus's decade at Tayma
entries.hint: For about ten years Nabonidus governed his empire from the oasis of Tayma in northern Arabia, occupying a string of oases down the incense road — Tayma, Dedan, Khaybar, Yathrib, Fadak — while his son Belshazzar held Babylon. Why is disputed: to control the caravan trade, to worship Sin away from the Marduk priests, to escape a plague or a coup. Cuneiform inscriptions of his are cut into the rock at Tayma, and a Dead Sea scroll remembers a Babylonian king struck ill in that place.
entries.note: Paul-Alain Beaulieu, 'The Reign of Nabonidus' (1989); the Tayma stelae (DAI excavations); the 'Prayer of Nabonidus' (4QPrNab); see the folio dedan-tayma-1200bc-300bc.

entries.label: The gathering of Persia
entries.hint: In a single decade Cyrus the Persian overthrew his Median overlord (550), conquered Croesus of Lydia and the Greek cities of the Aegean coast (546), and secured the Iranian plateau — leaving Babylon, alienated from its own priesthood by Nabonidus, encircled and alone. The Nabonidus Chronicle tracks Cyrus's campaigns year by year with mounting alarm. When he turned south in 539, the outcome was not in serious doubt.
entries.note: Pierre Briant, 'From Cyrus to Alexander: A History of the Persian Empire' (2002); the Nabonidus Chronicle (ABC 7).

entries.label: The Cyrus Cylinder and the propaganda of liberation
entries.hint: Cyrus buried in Babylon's wall a clay barrel inscribed, in fluent Babylonian, with the claim that Marduk himself had searched the lands for a righteous king, chosen Cyrus, and delivered Babylon into his hands 'without battle' to end the impieties of Nabonidus. Cyrus returned the deported gods to their cities and, in the biblical tradition, let the Judean exiles go home. It is a conqueror's masterpiece of local legitimation — and, misread, the 'first charter of human rights'.
entries.note: Amélie Kuhrt, 'The Cyrus Cylinder and Achaemenid Imperial Policy' (JSOT 1983); Irving Finkel (ed.), 'The Cyrus Cylinder' (2013).
